story: A flexing muscle looked like a mouse moving under the skin: Greek mûs means both mouse and muscle, and Latin musculus, our "muscle", means "little mouse".
Roman candidates for office wore a toga whitened with chalk, the toga candida, so a candidate is literally "one dressed in white".
Melancholy is "black bile": ancient medicine blamed sadness on an excess of it, one of the four humours.
Rubbed amber attracts light objects. In 1600 William Gilbert coined Latin electricus, "like amber", for the effect, from Greek ēlektron, "amber".
A companion is someone you share bread with (com- "with" + panis "bread").
Sarcasm comes from Greek sarkazein, from sarx "flesh": "to tear flesh", or to gnash the teeth in anger. A sarcophagus is a "flesh-eater": the limestone was believed to consume the bodies laid in it.
Trivial comes from trivium, a place where three roads meet, and so something ordinary or commonplace.
A disaster is literally a "bad star": misfortune was once blamed on an unfavourable position of the planets.
An idiot was originally a "private person", a layman who took no part in public life (Greek idiōtēs).
Lunatic reflects the old belief that madness came and went with the phases of the moon.
Someone innocent is literally "not harming" (in- + nocere).
A villain was originally a farm labourer on a villa, a country estate. The meaning slid from "peasant" to "scoundrel" through upper-class contempt.
The dandelion is named for its jagged leaves: French dent de lion, "lion's tooth".
Wealth was once counted in head of livestock, which is why "cattle" and "chattel" both come from Latin capitale, from caput "head", as does capital.
Hysteria was named in the belief that it was caused by a disturbance of the womb.
Edward Jenner protected people against smallpox with cowpox (variolae vaccinae, "cow pox"), which gave us the word vaccine.
Romans counted with small pebbles, calculi, which gave us calculate. Doctors still call kidney stones calculi.
A monster was originally a monstrum, a divine omen or warning, from monere, "to warn".
Greek biblos, "papyrus, book", is named after Byblos, the Phoenician port that exported papyrus to Greece.
Greek athletes trained naked, so a gymnasium was literally a "place for exercising naked".
A pedagogue was a slave who walked children to school. An encyclopedia comes from Greek enkyklios paideia, "all-round education".
Nausea comes from Greek naus, "ship": it first meant seasickness.
A holocaust was originally a sacrifice "burnt whole" (Greek holos + kaustos).
Greek kosmos meant "order" and also "ornament", which is why the universe (an ordered whole) and cosmetics share a root.
Clinic comes from the related Greek klinē, "bed": clinical medicine was taught at the patient's bedside.
A hypocrite was originally a stage actor, Greek hypokritēs: someone playing a part.
Alfred Nobel named his invention dynamite from Greek dynamis, "power". His fortune from it later funded the Nobel Prizes.
Roman priests foretold the future by watching birds, so something auspicious was literally "bird-watched" and found favourable (avis + specere).
Virtue first meant "manliness" or valour, from Latin vir, "man".
Latin virus meant "poison" or "slimy liquid" long before anyone could see the particles we now call viruses.
Egregious means "out of the flock". It first meant "outstanding" in a good way, and only later took on its bad sense.
To record is literally to "bring back to the heart": Latin recordari, "to remember". We still learn things "by heart".
A mortgage is literally a "dead pledge" (Old French mort gage, translating Medieval Latin mortuum vadium).
Pedigree comes from French pied de grue, "crane's foot", after the branching lines on family-tree charts.
The Occident (the West) is where the sun "falls", from occidere, "to fall, set".
The Orient (the East) is where the sun rises, from oriri, "to rise".
"Nice" comes from Latin nescius, "not knowing", and once meant foolish before drifting to its modern sense.
A president is literally "one who sits in front", presiding over a meeting.
Recipe is Latin for "take!": the first word of a doctor's prescription, later used for cooking instructions.
The solstice is when the sun seems to "stand still" (sol + sistere) before its path turns back.
An insect is "cut into" segments: a Latin translation of Greek entomon, which gives us entomology.
An atom is literally "uncuttable", the smallest possible piece. Atoms were later split anyway.
Economy was originally "household management" (Greek oikos "house" + nemein "to manage, distribute").
An architect is a "chief builder" (Greek arkhi- "chief" + tektōn "builder").
An epidemic is a disease "upon the people", spreading through a population.
Philadelphia, "the city of brotherly love", is Greek philos "loving" + adelphos "brother".
Television mixes Greek tele with Latin visio, and early critics complained that the hybrid word was bad Greek and bad Latin.
Hydrogen means "water-maker": burning it produces water.
Lavoisier named oxygen "acid-maker" because he wrongly believed every acid contained it.
An oxymoron, "sharp-dull", is itself an oxymoron.
An infant is literally "not speaking", from in- + fari, "to speak".
Spirit first meant "breath". To inspire was to breathe life (or an idea) into someone.
A file was originally a string or wire on which papers were hung to keep them in order (filum, "thread").
The Canary Islands were named Insula Canaria, "Island of Dogs", and the birds are named after the islands.
A verse is a "turning", like a plough turning at the end of a row to start the next line.
A peninsula is "almost an island" (paene + insula).
Insulin is named after the islets of Langerhans, the "little islands" of cells in the pancreas that make it.
Carnival possibly comes from Italian carnevale, "removing meat": the feast before the meatless days of Lent. Other origins have been proposed.
The Mediterranean is the sea "in the middle of the land" (medius + terra).
In Rome an album was a white tablet on which public notices were written.
Latin sinister meant "left": the left side was considered unlucky, while dexterity comes from the right hand.
Ambition comes from ambire, "to go around": Roman candidates went around canvassing for votes.
A monk is "one who lives alone", from Greek monachos, "solitary".
A patriot loves the patria, the "fatherland".
A sinecure is a job "without care", that pays without real duties. It was first a church post with no souls to care for.
Sanguine means hopeful: blood was the humour believed to make people cheerful.
Malaria is Italian mala aria, "bad air": the disease was blamed on swamp air before mosquitoes were understood.
Strategy is literally "generalship", from Greek stratēgos, "army leader".
Raphael Lemkin coined "genocide" in 1944 from Greek genos "race" and Latin -cidium "killing".
An autopsy is literally "seeing for oneself" (Greek autos + opsis).
A biscuit is literally "twice cooked" (French bis cuit).
Preposterous literally means "before-behind" (prae + posterus), back to front.
October was the eighth month in the old Roman calendar, which began in March. The same goes for September (seven), November (nine) and December (ten).
To decimate first meant to kill one soldier in ten, a Roman punishment for mutiny.
Quintessence is the "fifth essence": the ether that ancient philosophers believed filled the heavens, beyond the four elements of earth, water, air and fire.
Lucifer means "light-bearer" (lux + ferre) and was originally a name for the morning star, Venus.
A verdict is literally a "true saying" (vere dictum).
